title: Anand at dusk
hook: the six pauris also sit inside the evening Rehras

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand Karaj, and your line, end in bliss. Did you close one ordinary thing on purpose? Today, the same six pauris, not at a ceremony, but at the end of an ordinary day. Day four hundred three.

Play a song you love at seven in the morning, on the way to work, coffee in hand. Then play the same song at seven in the evening, shoes off, lights low. It's the same recording, note for note. But it isn't the same song. In the morning it pushes you out the door. In the evening it brings you home. A Sikh who keeps the daily prayers meets the Anand twice a day, in two different lights. Today: anand bhaiaa.
screen: `ONE SONG AT 7 A.M.` → `THE SAME SONG AT 7 P.M.` → `THE ANAND, TWICE A DAY.`

segments.voice: In the morning, the Rehat Maryada names the Japji, Jaap Sahib and the savaiyas, and many Sikhs add the whole Anand, all forty pauris, to those morning banis. That's the full meal. Then evening comes, and with it Rehras, the evening prayer, which we'll walk through line by line starting in two days. Near its end, Rehras carries the same six pauris you now know: the first five, and the fortieth. So the Anand frames the day. It's there at the start, in full, and it returns at dusk, shorter, like a taste of the morning's meal. Think about what the first line sounds like at each end. Anand bhaiaa meree maae: joy has come, my mother, I have found the True Guru. In the morning, that line goes out into the day ahead, before anything has gone right or wrong. At dusk, the day has happened. The bus was late. Someone was unkind. Something good came out of nowhere. And still the same words come: joy has come, mother. Not because the day was perfect. The line says where the joy comes from: I have found the True Guru. Not from the day. That's why it can be sung at both ends. Some families sing the evening pauris together, standing in a kitchen, or sitting on the floor of a front room with the lamps just lit. Some say them alone on a train home. The words don't change. The light does. Dusk, with joy.
screen: `MORNING: ALL FORTY PAURIS.` · `DUSK: THE SIX PAURIS INSIDE REHRAS.` · `THE SAME FIRST LINE AT BOTH ENDS.` · `THE JOY: FROM THE GURU, NOT THE DAY.` · then, large: `DUSK, WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum the first pauri at dusk. If it's evening where you are, look at the light outside. If it isn't, just picture the sky going orange. Then hum, or softly say, the first line: anand bhaiaa meree maae, satguroo mai paaiaa. Joy has come, my mother, I have found the True Guru. Let your whole day so far stand behind the words, the good and the bad. Say it, or hum it, two or three times. Then rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Anand bhaiaa, joy has come. The six pauris of the Anand return inside Rehras, the evening prayer, so the song of bliss frames the Sikh day at both ends.
Your line: dusk, with joy. Tonight, as the light goes, hum anand bhaiaa once, whatever kind of day it was. Day four hundred three.

original.note: Gurmukhi: anand bhaiaa, joy has come; the opening of the Anand, said in the morning and again at dusk.

trapdoor: what you thought: Anand at dusk means a second, different evening hymn of joy.
what it means: the same six pauris return inside Rehras, so the song of bliss holds both ends of the day.

what a scholar hears: the Rehat Maryada's morning banis are the Japji, Jaap and the ten savaiyas, and it sets the six pauris within Rehras; the full Anand in the morning comes from the wider five-bani practice many Sikhs keep.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on nitnem: the morning banis and Rehras

notes: Morning banis per the Rehat Maryada: Japji, Jaap, Tav Prasad Savaiye, Chaupai, Anand Sahib. Confirm, and that Rehras includes the first five and the fortieth pauris of Anand.
Some traditions recite the full Anand in the morning; others vary. Phrased as 'many Sikhs'.
Pauri 1 paraphrased as 'joy has come, my mother, I have found the True Guru'. Confirm.

Review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: the teach and trapdoor said the Anand is one of 'the five morning banis' listed by the Rehat Maryada; its morning nitnem is Japji, Jaap and the ten savaiyas, with the full Anand (and Chaupai) a widely kept addition. The narrator's 'the joy was never coming from the day' now ties to what the first line says. Keeper: the earlier note listing five morning banis 'per the Rehat Maryada' looks wrong; confirm.
